analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for the President or Vice President to sell nonpublic government information.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2026 with six Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, the bill has sat untouched in the House Judiciary Committee ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime for the President or Vice President to sell or exchange nonpublic government information for money, and would punish anyone who knowingly buys it. Penalties include fines up to double the transaction's value, up to five years in prison, forfeiture of profits, and civil suits by the Attorney General to claw back gains. It also covers businesses the President or Vice President control or own at least 5% of, and pauses the legal deadline for bringing cases while they hold office.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors and citizens who depend on government information being released publicly, on equal terms, gain a rule that stops the White House from selling secrets to insiders. The Treasury also collects the fines and civil penalties. Anyone competing in markets where a privileged tip from the President could move prices benefits from a level field.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Citizens relying on equal access to information

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new federal crime barring the President and Vice President from selling or exchanging nonpublic information they gain through their office for financial benefit, punishable by a fine of up to double the transaction's value, up to five years in prison, or both, plus forfeiture of any proceeds.

Lets the Attorney General bring a civil case — even without a criminal prosecution — to disgorge all profits and impose a penalty of up to the greater of $250,000 or three times the gain, using a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard and a six-year window that is tolled while the official holds office.

Extends the ban to covered entities — businesses controlled by the President or Vice President or in which they own at least 5% — and holds counterparties who knowingly provide anything of value jointly and severally liable.

Requires the Office of Government Ethics to refer credible evidence to the Attorney General and to notify the House and Senate Judiciary Committees of each referral, creating a paper trail outside the Justice Department's discretion.

Expressly covers official statements distributed through application programming interfaces or other means not made available to the general public on equal terms, aimed at channels that give some market participants faster access to a President's words than everyone else.

analysis.who_pays: The President and Vice President, their family-controlled or 5%-owned businesses, and anyone who knowingly buys or brokers their nonpublic information would face fines, prison, forfeiture, and civil clawbacks. The Justice Department would bear the cost of enforcement.
analysis.who_pays_short: President, Vice President, and information buyers

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only the President and Vice President — not members of Congress, judges, or other executive officials — despite a name that echoes broader congressional stock-trading bans, so most officeholders' trading and information-selling would remain governed by existing, weaker rules.

Enforcement depends almost entirely on the Attorney General, who serves at the President's pleasure; an administration could simply decline to bring criminal or civil cases, leaving the referral requirement as the only outside check.

The definition of nonpublic information is broad — it sweeps in anything a covered person knows or reasonably should know is not public, including communications not released 'on equal terms' — which opponents could argue is vague or overbroad and invite constitutional challenge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill closes a real gap: there is no general criminal statute today barring the President or Vice President from selling nonpublic information for money, and the remedy is cheap for the public because fines flow to the Treasury. Its honest weaknesses are narrowness (two officeholders covered, everyone else untouched) and reliance on an Attorney General who may lack the will to enforce the law against the administration. As drafted it is a modest, targeted fix rather than a comprehensive trading ban.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it, so it has never come to a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Andrea Salinas introduced the bill on August 6, 2026, joined as original cosponsors by Reps. Mfume, Bynum, and Norton.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and the action record shows nothing since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
Six Democratic cosponsors have signed on; no Republican has, and with a closely divided House the bill has no path to the floor without majority-party support.
If it dies without action by January 3, 2027, the sale of nonpublic information by the President or Vice President remains lawful under federal criminal law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, executive insiders are better off: the President and Vice President remain free to sell nonpublic information for financial benefit, and anyone positioned to buy it keeps that advantage, because the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Executive insiders and information buyers, so far

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; no vote has occurred, so the split is so far entirely on sponsorship lines.

industries.industry: Traders and investors who buy privileged information
industries.note: The bill criminalizes knowingly paying for nonpublic information from the President or Vice President and attaches joint liability to counterparties, cutting off a channel of private market advantage that ordinary investors cannot access.

industries.industry: Businesses controlled by or 5%-owned by the President or Vice President
industries.note: Covered entities would be barred from selling nonpublic information for financial benefit and exposed to forfeiture, disgorgement, and civil penalties of up to triple the gain.

The bill's express coverage of official statements released through APIs or other unequal channels targets arrangements that let some traders act on a President's words before the public can; those operations would lose their edge, while markets overall would price information more evenly.

analysis.trajectory: With roughly five months left in this Congress, no committee action since referral, six cosponsors, and no Republican support, the bill is very likely to die in the Judiciary Committee without a vote, as most private members' bills do; a floor vote would require the majority party to schedule it, and nothing in the record suggests that will happen.
